cells.tense: You are reading how a shared thing holds together, right now, while it is still being lived.
cells.act: let yourself want it, plainly, to yourself
cells.ask: Among the customs and handed-down ways you keep, name to yourself the one you'd grieve most to lose, and admit you want it kept — no plan, no announcement.
cells.core:
You can stand inside something shared and see how it works at the same time. When you read the grain of a custom or a way a group does things, the pattern holds you up rather than flattening the people in it — you get the mechanism and the meaning both, and it tends to leave people freer, not smaller. Take the thing apart and it comes back more alive than you found it.

From here, admit you want it. Among the things you keep — a phrase, a habit, a way of marking a day — want one of them clearly, with nothing decided after it. That want isn't an argument for keeping everything; it just marks what's actually yours. From it you get something to steer the rest by. What stays unresolved can stay that way rather longer than feels settled.

cells.tense: You will keep building the pattern out, and the structure you make will start running past what it was meant to hold.
cells.act: set one rule that makes the rest easier
cells.ask: For the shared practice you can't stop turning over, decide one rule — the order, the hour, who takes which part — and put it where the others can find it.
cells.core:
The pattern-seeing is running hot. You're working out how a shared thing functions so exhaustively that the explanation starts replacing the thing: what someone meant, whether it was safe, what the gesture was really doing — you're three layers down before the moment is over, and the analysis keeps grinding with nothing left to solve. The tired version is a rhythm where you know every dynamic of the group and nobody there knows you're holding the whole reading.

So settle one rule. Take the shared situation you can't stop turning over and choose a single thing — a sequence, an hour, who handles what — and stop there. That rule is not for the pattern; it's so the others can see what they're inside of. Speaking it plainly will cost less than the quiet accounting.

cells.tense: You were near things you stopped looking inside of, and the surface is all that stayed.
cells.act: learn how the people before you did it
cells.ask: Choose one thing the people near you do a certain way, and learn how it was done before them — one question asked, one account read. No conclusion required.
cells.core:
The shared thing isn't asking you to believe anything. Where you stand is literal, and depth has been keeping its distance: what a custom was for, what a phrase could carry, what a gesture was doing — none of that is reachable right now, and nothing has felt missing. The present is narrow here, and a good deal of what you move through stays on the surface you can see.

Widen it by learning one piece of the older way. Find out how something done by those near you was done before they got to it — ask, or read a single account — and leave the learning without interpretation. You don't have to agree with any of it or adopt it. What you get is contact with the line behind the practice, which is open to anyone willing to look, whether or not they belong.

cells.tense: You are moving through shared patterns you aren't tracking, while the pen is already in your hand.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: When a conversation gets hard this week, don't reach for the frame that explains it. Stay in the exchange through the difficult stretch, saying less, and give the other person their own account.
cells.core:
The patterns are steering you and you don't have a name for them — that's the honest read. The customs and habits you move through, the ways a group or a family does things, have a shape that shapes you, and it runs below where you can see it. So the reading keeps catching things you didn't put there, and you file those under the situation.

The other half is closeness without losing your own side. When a conversation gets hard, stay in the exchange through the difficult stretch rather than reaching for the analysis that would explain it. Say less. Don't fix it. Don't take the other person's account over, and don't hand them yours. What you get is the pattern showing itself live rather than in your read of it.

A reader could reasonably say their situation is the reverse — they're outside the shared thing, not carrying it — and the Too Little cell must not assert they were ever inside. The asks survive being wrong because each one works on something already present: a thing learned, a shape written down, a moment of pause, a conversation kept. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line implying I know what they've inherited rather than only what the card's mechanism does.
